content.thinking:
I need to avoid inserting my own figures and stick to names in braces. There's a timing discrepancy I'm puzzling over: the flag change timestamp of 15:29:26Z comes after the 15:24 onset, yet the investigator noted zero production changes in the 24 hours before 15:24 — so I need to reconcile how the flag toggle fits into that timeline.

Looking at the evaluation logs, the flag was fully on at 15:22-15:23, then started shifting at 15:24 toward a mixed and eventually fully-off state, with the recorded change timestamp trailing the actual behavior shift — I'm flagging this as an unexplained discrepancy to note rather than resolve. Recovery happened when the flag was reverted back to on at 15:29:41.

Now I'm building the causal chain: users experienced failed account pages with elevated error rates (citing the alert and relevant logs), traced to a ZeroDivisionError at a specific line in spend_summary.py, and I'm working through why that error occurred next.

The division fails because the monthly average calculation divides by the count of purchases this month, which is zero for shoppers with no purchases — though I'm treating this as an unverified static reading from a test helper rather than confirmed behavior. The flag being off routed more traffic down this vulnerable monthly-summary path, and since there were zero deploys in that window, the flag change stands as the only plausible trigger, even though the connection between the flag and the code path is only established through timing correlation rather than a direct reference in the repo. As contributing factors, I'm noting the absence of test coverage for idle shoppers and the lack of any staged rollout or guardrail on the flag change, which let it jump straight to 100% off.

Now I'm thinking through detection timing — the error logs show elevated rates starting around 15:22, so I want to quantify the delay between onset and when the alert actually fired, while avoiding fabricating specific numeric values. For action items, I'm proposing a canary/percent-rollout guard with error-rate monitoring for future flag toggles, plus noting that the revert is just a workaround since the underlying fix remains open. For lessons learned, the fast revert was a good outcome, though it's somewhat lucky that the system still functions correctly only because the flag happens to be back on.

There's also a timestamp discrepancy in the assumptions worth flagging, and the fix stays latent until it's properly merged. I'll keep the executive summary free of specific numbers, using placeholders instead, and move on to drafting it.

action_items.item: Add a regression test, if the draft fix does not already carry it, that the monthly average for a shopper with no purchases this month returns a defined value and the account page renders. Run it in CI for both flag states.
Make changes to legacy-checkout-fallback, and flags like it, roll out in stages. Hold each stage while the account-page error rate is watched, and roll back automatically if it rises.
Add a dashboard annotation or alert that shows flag changes next to the error rate for the service. Responders then see a flag toggle as a likely trigger as soon as the error rate rises.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers got errors instead of their account page. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average over {duration}, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have, and that was enough to page.

The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 while building the account page. The error appears from the onset and keeps recurring until the end of the window.

The line divides this month's spend by the number of purchases made this month. For a shopper with no purchases this month that number is zero, and the division fails. The code has no guard for that case. Code-Fix describes this as the ordinary case for shoppers. This comes from a static reading of the source that nothing ran, so it is unverified. It is consistent with the traceback.

More requests reached that monthly-summary path once the legacy-checkout-fallback flag was switched off. Flag evaluations were all on before the onset. At the onset they split between off and on, then went to all off. The flag change was the only change seen: the deploy and release query returned no production changes, so a deploy is ruled out. The error rate returned to normal once Argus set the flag back on. The record does not show how the flag routes requests into the monthly path. That link rests on timing, the recovery, and Code-Fix's unverified reading.

The flag could be switched off with the monthly path still unsafe for idle-this-month shoppers. The record does not show a test or check that covered this case before the flip, and the evidence does not go further than that.

contributing_factors.factor: The monthly average had no handling for a shopper with no purchases this month. No test for that case was seen in the record. The tests were added only with the proposed fix, which is not yet merged.

The flag moved from fully on to fully off within a few minutes. No canary, staged rollout or error-rate guard on the flag change was seen in the record. A flag change that broke account pages therefore reached all traffic before anyone reacted.

Detection took time. The paging rule waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding. The alert fired {alert_raised - began} after the onset. Nothing linked the flag change to the rise in errors until the Investigator read the flag history.
The mitigation only restores the flag. The defect stays in the code until the fix is merged, so switching the flag off again would bring the failures back.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, a share of shoppers on the shop got an error instead of their account page. Normally {errors_before} of requests fail. While the fault lasted {errors_while_broken} failed on average and {errors_at_worst} at the worst point. A feature flag was switched off, and that sent more account-page requests down a code path with a bug. The bug breaks the page for any shopper who has not bought anything this month, which is a common case. Argus switched the flag back on, and the error rate returned to normal. The underlying bug is still in the code. A draft fix has been proposed and has not yet been reviewed or merged.

got_lucky: The old flag setting still worked, so turning it back on was a safe and immediate mitigation. The bug stays latent for as long as the flag stays on, and nothing seen in the record stops someone switching it off again.
went_well: Argus formed a candidate within seconds of the page, tied it to the flag change, and reverted the flag. The error rate was back to normal by {back_to_normal}.
The mitigation was confirmed against the metrics, not assumed: the service was no longer at the incident's level after the revert.
A draft fix was proposed with tests that fail against the current code.
went_wrong: The bug sat in a common path, and no test for it was seen in the record. A flag flip was enough to expose it to a large share of users.
The revert only works around the bug, which stays in the code until the proposed fix is merged.
The change record for the flag toggle carries a time later than the onset, so the change history alone did not line up with the start of the errors.

input.root_cause: The monthly spend average in spend_summary.py divides by the number of purchases a shopper made this month. That number is zero for a shopper who has bought before but not this month, so the call raises ZeroDivisionError and the account page fails. Switching the legacy-checkout-fallback flag off sent more account-page requests down that path. The division by zero comes from a static reading of the code (F1) that nothing ran, so it is unverified. The traceback location does match it.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for a share of shoppers
